preamble: Deaffrication of the postalveolar ejective affricate [tʃʼ] to the alveolo-palatal ejective fricative [ɕʼ] in Kabardian (East Circassian). In words where literary Adyghe (West Circassian) кӏ [tʃʼ] continues Proto-Circassian *tʃʼ, literary Kabardian has щӏ [ɕʼ]: Adyghe кӏэ [t͡ʃʼa] 'new' corresponds to Kabardian щӏэ [ɕʼa]. Wiktionary reconstructs Proto-Circassian *t͡ʃʼa 'new' and *pt͡ʃʼəħ 'dream' with the affricate. Nikolayev & Starostin (1994: 199) list two Proto-Adyghe-Kabardian glottalized affricates, *č̣ and *č̣́, that stay affricates in Bzhedug and Temirgoy Adyghe but both appear as ṣ́ in Kabardian. The related West Caucasian languages also have an affricate here: Starling gives Abkhaz a-č̣á and Abaza č̣a 'young, fresh' and Ubykh č̣a 'good' beside Proto-Adyghe-Kabardian *č̣́a 'new', and notes that Ubykh č̣ regularly corresponds to Circassian č̣́. Wikipedia's Proto-Circassian article, which writes *t͡ʃʼ as чӏ (literary Adyghe кӏ), calls the change spirantization, lists the West Circassian Abzakh dialect as also affected, with щӏ [ɕʼ] or a weakened ӏь [ʔʲ], and the East Circassian Besleney dialect as unaffected, and has the retroflex *t͡ʂʼ (literary Adyghe чӏ) merge into the same ɕʼ, as in Adyghe гъучӏы : Kabardian гъущӏ 'iron' (Wikipedia, Circassian languages; Starling ʁʷǝč̣ǝ : ʁʷǝṣ́); that branch is not covered here because the atlas has no symbol for [ʈʂʼ]. Kabardian ɕʼ also has a source that is not [tʃʼ]: for the 'ten' set (Adyghe пшӏы : Kabardian пщӏы, both written ṗṣ́ǝ by Starling), Kuipers, as reported by Nikolayev & Starostin (1994: 197), reconstructs a glottalized fricative, and Nikolayev & Starostin themselves a glottalized hissing-hushing affricate *ć̣ that became a fricative in both languages. Kabardian кӏэ 'tail', from Proto-Circassian *kʲʼa (Wiktionary), did not take part.

examples.note: Wiktionary. Starling: Proto-Adyghe-Kabardian *č̣́a, Adyghe č̣́a, Kabardian ṣ́a; Abkhaz a-č̣á, Abaza č̣a 'young, fresh' and Ubykh č̣a 'good' keep an affricate. The same morpheme is in Kabardian щӏымахуэ [ɕʼəmaːxʷa] 'winter', which Wiktionary derives from щӏэ 'new' + махуэ 'day' (Proto-Circassian чӏымахуэ in Wikipedia's Proto-Circassian article).
Wikipedia (Proto-Circassian language), which gives пащӏэ for Abzakh as well. Adyghe пакӏэ 'whisker, mustache' and its IPA from Wiktionary.
Wikipedia (Proto-Circassian language), with Abzakh ӏегъуэжьын showing the weakening to [ʔʲ]. Wiktionary spells the Kabardian verb щӏегъуэжын [ɕʼeʁʷaʑən] and gives Adyghe кӏэгъожьын as its cognate.
